Exponents and thresholds

SymbolDefinitionStatusNotes
μ_maxTransverse Floquet exponent of Γ. Vol II Lemma 3.1 gives only its sign (μ_max < 0, "Floquet theory, [1] Thm 3.3"), for each system separately; it gives no value and no uniformity in z. Toy value −2 is the z → ∞ limit of the explicit linearization λ(z) = −2 + 2e^(−z), which is monotone decreasing in z (0 at z = 0, negative only for z > 0), so the limit exists there by the formula.
on 22 pages of this book
OPENOpen: for a general dm³ system, what μ_max is as a limit (lim, limsup or sup over z) and why it exists. Lemma 3.1 does not supply that; Book 4 ch10 calls its proof "numerical". Pages that state μ or μ_max as a z → ∞ / regularized limit, and so rely on this row (keyword match, 7): book1/vol2-dashboard.html, vol2-contact.html, vol2-toymodel.html, book4/ch03.html, book4/ch06b.html, book4/ch10.html, book7/ch-grothendieck.html. Not edited.
τEmbodiment threshold: τ = √(c/κ_noise), from the stochastic Lyapunov condition LV ≤ −cV + κ_noise‖σ‖², with κ_noise = ½ sup‖Hess V‖. The noise amplitude below which the system is stochastically stable. Toy value 2.
on 28 pages of this book
DEFINED in the papers + VERIFIED (toy value)Source: Vol II Thm 3.2 (citing GCM Def 3.4); Vol I §2 states τ = √(c/κ). Toy with V = ρ²: c = 4, Hess V = 2, κ_noise = 1, τ = 2 (recomputed). OPEN detail: Vol I says c = 1, κ = 1/4 (same ratio 4, different split); with its own W = ½ρ² the recomputed τ is 2.83, not 2. Which V is canonical is the author's call. Correction 2026-09-30: this row first said OPEN / no formula found. Wrong — my term scan missed a definition written as a formula. Checked 2026-10-01 against Vol I v7 §13.2 and the toy model: Vol I states c = 1, κ = 1/4 and τ = √(c/κ) = 2, but its toy drift is ρ̇ = −2ρ − 3ρ² − ρ³ with W = ½ρ², which gives Ẇ ≈ −4W near Γ, so c = 4 for W, and κ_noise = ½·sup‖Hess W‖ = ½ at Hess W = 1, so τ = √8. A time rescaling t → λt would need the linear rate to be −ρ/2, but it is −2ρ, so a time-unit convention does not explain (1, ¼). Still OPEN: no derivation of (1, ¼) found. Possible reading, not found in Vol I (arithmetic only): any c at or below the sharp decay rate is a valid constant in LV ≤ −cV + κ_noise‖σ‖², so (1, ¼) would be valid, not sharp, for V = ρ²/4 (κ_noise = ¼): the sharp pair for that V is (4, ¼) with τ = 4, and c = 1 gives τ = 2. Vol I names its Lyapunov function as W = ½ρ², not ρ²/4, and says nowhere how c = 1 was chosen, so this stays a hypothesis. Consequence for the definition: τ is fixed only by V together with the sharp c; for V = ρ² the Vol II pair (4, 1) is sharp and τ = 2 stands.
τ normalizationτ is not invariant under rescaling V: for V → λV, c is unchanged, κ_noise scales by λ, so τ → τ/√λ (τ·√λ = 2 for every λ in the toy model). V = ρ² is canonical (author's confirmation, 2026-09-30): it is the V of Vol II Thm 3.2 / GCM Def 3.4 and gives τ = 2.
on 28 pages of this book
DECIDED (V) + VERIFIED (scaling law)Explains 2 versus 2.83: W = ½ρ² is λ = ½, so τ = 2√2. τ is a V-dependent bound, not an intrinsic threshold: "σ < τ" is a sufficient condition from one Lyapunov function. Neither Vol I v7 nor Vol II v2aa claims it is sharp (Vol II's equivalence is only "finite and positive iff"; Vol I §13.2 says τ = 2 is specific to the toy model). Sharpness for ρ² is unchecked. Vol I's split (c, κ) = (1, 1/4): stated in §13.2 with no derivation (only place found; Vol II not searched for it); c = 4 for every λρ², so it is not a rescaling of V. Erratum on hold: do not write "different normalization" for that split; say it is unexplained unless a derivation turns up. Independent support: MASTER.tex lists "Lyapunov function V = (r−1)²" among the derived objects "consistent across all papers"; that is V = ρ².

on 3 pages of this book
OPENA bound of 9/4 is above 1, so the step to 5/9 carries the whole claim and is asserted. Note the three κ's in Vol I: curvature κ(s), noise coefficient κ in τ = √(c/κ), and this contraction κ. They are different quantities; the chain is not a transformation rule for the noise κ.
W(Γ)Winding integral: W(Γ) = ∮_Γ λ, the raw line integral of the primitive λ (dλ = ω) around the limit cycle, with no 1/2π normalization; by Stokes it is the symplectic area Γ encloses. Toy model: W = ∮ r² dθ = 2πr₀² = 2π at r₀ = 1.
on 3 pages of this book
DEFINED in the papers (source found)Source: Proposition "Topological invariance of ∮_Γ λ" (prop:winding) in master_book_FINAL_v2.tex and completePrincipia.tex (Downloads): independent of the choice of λ, invariant under admissible operators, nonzero when Γ bounds no chain; proof by Stokes. Finding: that proposition never says W is an integer. "W(Γ) ∈ ℤ" (GCM page, Theorem A(ii)) appears to be an addition there and is false as stated (2πr₀²). Fix the claim, not the definition; the author decides how. Also worth checking: proof (i) uses ∮ df = 0, but two primitives of ω differ by a closed form, not necessarily an exact one; independence of λ needs that difference exact along Γ (e.g. Γ contractible or H¹ = 0).

DECIDEDPer the 2026-09-29 audit entry; Institutional Edition App. A g–L–R–U is a different set of objects.
dm³The contact 3-manifold (X, α) with α = dz − ρ²dθ (more generally α = dz − λ, dλ = ω) carrying a hyperbolic limit cycle Γ, with the operator chain G = U∘F∘K∘C acting on it; the same structure expressed across many domains and scales. It is the minimal case, generalized to contact (2n+1)-manifolds in the GCM framework (base M arbitrary, M̂ = M × ℝ; Theorem C on ℝ^(2n+1)). The toy ODE is one vector field on the 3-manifold.DECIDED (author, 2026-09-30)Vol I Fig. 3: "Dimension 3 is the minimum in which this structure is non-trivial (§16)." The GCM page's "dm³ system" (M, g, Γ, V, ξ) is the generalized setting; for n = 1 the base M is the 2-dimensional (r, θ) plane.
dm³ / dm3 (naming)Write dm³ in prose and on grant and site pages; dm3 is the ASCII alias in code, filenames and Lean identifiers. Define it once here; other pages point to this row instead of restating it.DECIDED (author, 2026-09-30)A convention.
